summary.text: The Deccan Traps are a large igneous province in west-central India, made of many stacked layers of solidified flood basalt.
The eruptions ran for roughly 600,000 to 800,000 years around 66 million years ago, spanning the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary.
They were once proposed as a major cause of the Cretaceous–Paleogene mass extinction, but most scientists now credit the Chicxulub impact and give the lava a minor role at most.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: More than about 2 kilometres of basalt layers

facts.label: Original area
facts.value: Up to 1.5 million km², about half of India

items.prompt: Geologists call vast stacked lava fields like these "traps". Where does that word come from?

options.label: An English word, since lava caught animals
A Sanskrit word meaning southern lands
A Swedish word for stairs, for the stepped hills
A Latin word meaning hard black rock

items.explain: Trap comes from the Swedish trapp, meaning stairs, describing the step-like hills of the landscape.

items.prompt: The extinction 66 million years ago looks sudden and simultaneous on land and at sea. Why does that count against the Deccan lava as its main cause?

options.label: Lava cannot reach the ocean, so sea life was safe
Long eruptions should cause staggered losses
The lava had stopped erupting long before then
Volcanic gases only ever warm the climate

items.explain: A large igneous province would be expected to cause staggered extinctions, while a sudden, global, simultaneous die-off fits an impact.

items.prompt: Gases such as sulfur dioxide poured out while the Deccan Traps formed. Which way did the temperature move in that period?

options.label: It dropped by about 2 °C on average
It rose by about 2 °C on average
It rose by about 10 °C on average
It stayed the same throughout

items.explain: Volcanic gases, especially sulfur dioxide, may have changed the climate, and an average drop of about 2 °C was recorded.

items.prompt: The lava flows you can see today cover only about a third of the area they once did. What shrank them?

options.label: The lava slowly sank back into the mantle
Rising seas flooded most of the old flows
Later eruptions melted the older lava away
Erosion and plate movements over time

items.explain: Erosion and plate tectonics cut the region from about 1.5 million km² to around 500,000 km² of visible flows.

items.prompt: The heat source thought to have made most of the Deccan Traps is still active today. Where does it build land now?

options.label: The Mascarene Islands in the Indian Ocean
The Hawaiian Islands in the Pacific Ocean
The island of Iceland in the North Atlantic
The Himalaya mountains north of India

items.explain: The Réunion hotspot, believed to have produced much of the Traps, formed the modern Mascarene Islands.

items.prompt: Why is it hard to pin down exactly how fast the Deccan lava piled up?

options.label: The rocks are far too old to date at all
Most of the lava has eroded completely away
Gaps between eruptions are shorter than dating can resolve
The flows contain no minerals that can be measured

items.explain: Transitions between eruptions may have lasted only a few thousand years, finer than dating methods can pinpoint, so the rate is hard to constrain.
